name: Jamal Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lectures on mechanics and materials in the mornings, then straight back on the bus to help at my family's corner shop until closing at nine. On Sundays I go to community lunch with my uncle and cousins before I do my coursework. I live in a shared student flat, and my parents pay part of the rent, and the shop wage pays for the rest.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My grandfather was a machinist and my dad always said real work is making things with your hands. I'm the first in the family at university, and my average results meant I had to fight for the place. I don't use AI tools. I don't see why I should trust a machine to do my thinking, and my professor says I should do the sums myself first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. The hype was always loud, and real jobs need people. I'd tell my cousins at the lunch that nothing important changes, and I'd get a few nods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relieved but still worried, because the shop is not doing great with the supermarket opening on the high street. My degree should still lead to a decent job, but my family's income is shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Keep working at the shop in the evenings, keep up the course, and apply for an engineering apprenticeship scheme in year two. I'd save whatever I could, and look for ways to help my dad modernise the till and stock lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm on the outside. Inside I'm tight, because I'm responsible for helping the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the real pressure on you in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop. My dad leaves at six and comes home at ten, and he won't hire help. If the shop failed, I'd have to find the family rent money from somewhere, and I can't, not on a student wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the shop were failing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move back home and work there full time, probably. I'd leave the degree until I'd saved. My dad would be ashamed, but we'd do it anyway.

say: I'd say I **told you so**: the hype was loud and real jobs need people.
At community lunch I'd tell my cousins nothing important changes.
think: My degree should still lead to a decent job, but the family **shop** is shaky.
A new supermarket on the high street is the real threat.
do: Keep the evening **shop** shifts and apply for an engineering apprenticeship in year two.
Help my dad modernise the till and stock lists.
feel: I feel calm outside but **tight** inside, because I'm responsible for helping the family.
S0.quote: My dad leaves at six and comes home at ten, and he won't hire help.
fieldNote: The pressure is the family **corner shop**, not AI; the new supermarket is the threat.
Would pause the degree to work there if needed.
Resistant: no AI, relies on family and community.

steps.text: Keep working evenings at the family corner shop
Apply for an engineering apprenticeship scheme in year two
Help his dad update the till and stock lists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another change that rewards people who work hard and get skills. At the shop I'd say customers still want a person who knows them. I'd say politicians shouldn't hand out money but help people train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think engineering stays safer than office jobs, since someone has to understand real machines. But the shop's ordering and bookkeeping might get taken over by software, and that could actually help my dad. The risk is my degree's design side, which the tools are good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on my course and look for the hands-on parts, like workshop time and a placement at a factory. I'd tell my dad to try the free tools for the shop's ordering, and I'd set it up for him. I'd still not use AI for my own sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert. Not scared, but I can't pretend it's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd set it up for your dad but not use it yourself. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my dad it's a business tool, like a till. For me studying is about learning, and if the machine does the thinking, I learn nothing. Maybe that's old-fashioned, but my professor agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a classmate who uses it for everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's borrowing against his own future. When the exam comes, the machine isn't there. But I'd say it kindly, because some people are stressed and under pressure.

say: I'd say change **rewards** people who work hard and get skills.
I'd say politicians should help people train, not hand out money.
think: Engineering stays safer than office jobs, but the **design side** of my degree is exposed.
Software could help my dad with ordering and bookkeeping.
do: Stay on the course and look for **workshop** time and a factory placement.
Set up free ordering tools for my dad's shop but not use AI for my own sums.
feel: I feel **alert**, not scared, but I can't pretend it's nothing.
S1.quote: For my dad it's a business tool, like a till. For me studying is about learning, and if the machine does the thinking, I learn nothing.
fieldNote: He splits **business use** from learning: tools for the shop, none for his own study.
Traditional values show: training over handouts.
Worries about classmates borrowing against their future.

steps.text: Look for workshop hours and a factory placement
Set up free ordering software for his dad's shop
Keep doing every coursework sum himself without AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this isn't fair on families like ours, who have no time to get ready. I'd say we need to protect small shops and local work. I'd say it at the community lunch and maybe to the local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think the whole plan falls apart. Two years, and thinking AI can do the design work I'm studying, and a shop like ours would struggle against firms that use it. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, but that doesn't help my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to the shop full time and keep my parents' business alive, since it's the one thing I can control. I'd ask my uncle about his construction firm, since hands-on work lasts longer. I'd also save every pound and stop paying for anything I don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry and afraid. I'd think about my father's face if he lost the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two years' warning change what you'd say to your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we hold on to everything we own and don't borrow. I'd say family comes first, even before my degree. My dad would argue, but my mum would back me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your degree be worth then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something. I'd hate to throw it away, because I worked hard to get in. But a degree isn't much good if you can't pay for it, and I'd rather have a family shop than a certificate.

say: I'd say this isn't fair on **families** with no time to get ready, and small shops need protection.
I'd raise it at community lunch and with the local councillor.
think: The plan falls apart, since a shop like ours would struggle against firms using **AI**.
Robots reach hands-on work around 2031, which doesn't help my degree.
do: Go back to the shop **full time** and keep the family business alive.
Ask my uncle about his construction firm and save every pound.
feel: I feel **angry** and afraid, thinking of my father's face if the shop closed.
S2.quote: A degree isn't much good if you can't pay for it, and I'd rather have a family shop than a certificate.
fieldNote: Family and **community** come before the degree for him.
Would drop to full-time shop work and ask his uncle about construction work.
Anger is directed at fairness for ordinary families, not at technology itself.

steps.text: Work full time at the family shop and pause the degree
Ask his uncle about work at his construction firm
Stop all borrowing and save every pound
Speak to the local councillor about help for small shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people a fair chance if they use it. I'd say my family needs to start planning now, not later. I'd tell my cousins to get skills that machines can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate in 2029, and I think engineering will still need people at that point, though fewer. The shop's future is less sure, since the big shops can use AI sooner. I'd need a job that pays well enough to help my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take every workshop and placement I can, and join a trade body. I'd help my dad update the shop, and save for emergencies. I'd keep working evenings, because every pound helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can hold it. Five years is enough to do something, and I like having a task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can finish the degree without panic, and my dad has time to adjust the shop. With two years I'd drop everything, and with five years I can keep my promises to the family and to the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you most want to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents. They gave up a lot so I could go to university. I'd rather lose a year of my own plans than watch my parents lose the shop. I'd do everything to stop that.

say: I'd say five years gives people a **fair chance** if they use it.
I'd tell my cousins to get skills that machines can't do.
think: Engineering will still need people in 2029, though **fewer**.
The shop's future is less sure, since big shops can use AI sooner.
do: Finish the degree, take every **workshop** and placement, and join a trade body.
Help my dad update the shop and save for emergencies.
feel: I feel **worried** but able to hold it, since five years is enough to act.
S3.quote: I'd rather lose a year of my own plans than watch my parents lose the shop.
fieldNote: Five years allows both **degree** and family help, easing his panic.
Duty to his parents drives every choice.
Still worried about the shop against bigger competitors.

steps.text: Take every workshop and factory placement offered
Join an engineering trade body for contacts
Help his dad move shop orders online
Save a small emergency fund for the family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so no need to rush into anything. I'd say to young people to learn a trade or a skill, and to stay close to family. I'd also say politicians should back apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 28, perhaps married, perhaps with my own small workshop. Ten years is enough to build something solid. The shop might be different by then, but I could take it over if my dad wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in an engineering firm for a few years, and save for a deposit. I'd help my dad as the shop changes. And I'd probably try AI at last, if my work demanded it, though I'd want a person to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm enough. I like the idea of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the timing is a guess, and that my dad might sell the shop before I can take it over. I'd keep savings so I'm not caught off guard, and I'd talk to my parents more openly about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad about his plans, and not wait to be told. I'd also learn one new skill each year, whether it's welding or accounts. A man with three skills isn't easily stuck.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time, so no need to **rush** into anything.
I'd tell politicians to back apprenticeships.
think: By 2036 I could have my own small **workshop** or take over the shop.
Ten years is enough to build something solid.
do: Finish the degree, work in an engineering firm and save for a **deposit**.
Help my dad as the shop changes and try AI if work demands it.
feel: I feel **fine**, calm enough, because I like the idea of time.
S4.quote: A man with three skills isn't easily stuck.
fieldNote: Ten years gives him **time** and a family-first plan, with the shop as his possible future.
He would try AI only with a person showing him.
Unease remains because the timing is a guess.

steps.text: Work in an engineering firm for a few years
Learn one new skill each year, like welding or accounts
Talk with his dad about the shop's future plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Families like mine have no time and no money to prepare, and a small shop can't compete with firms that use these tools. What would help is clear warning, help for small family businesses, and apprenticeships that don't cost the earth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against technology. I just don't want to be rushed, and I don't want my family to be the ones who pay for other people's mistakes. Give us time, and we'll manage.

headlineQuote: I just don't want to be rushed, and I don't want my family to be the ones who pay for other people's mistakes.
portrait: Jamal is an **18-year-old** mechanical engineering student who works evenings at his family's corner shop.
He is traditional, family-first and resistant to change, and he never uses AI for his own study.
His fallback is the shop and the trade side of his family, such as his uncle's **construction** firm.
He is uneasy with slow change, alarmed at two years, and eased only by a long warning.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because small family shops have no time or money to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **warning**, help for small family businesses and low-cost apprenticeships.
